records.name: Mpumalanga
records.current_summary: Mpumalanga is where the country's official house of traditional leaders launched its organised campaign against constitutional equality for queer people. Meeting at Hazyview in June 2010, the National House of Traditional Leaders and its provincial houses — while professing to 'respect' the Constitutional Court's same-sex marriage judgment — resolved that 'traditional leaders are disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts', declared their opposition to legal recognition, warned of ostracism and violence, and vowed a five-year campaign against it. Reporting in 2016 documented the same body asking Parliament to review the constitutional clause that protects people from discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.  This is official traditional-structure hostility, taken on this province's soil and stated as durable climate rather than enacted law: there is no provincial statute against queer people, no enforcement against visitors, and no retrieved Mpumalanga-specific trans-incident series. The finding is the platform the country's chiefhood announced here — and did not retract.

sources.claim: Published letter (June 2010) from the NHTL and its Provincial Houses after meeting at Hazyview, Mpumalanga: while 'respecting' the Constitutional Court same-sex marriage judgment, 'traditional leaders are disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts'; states they do not support legalisation of same-sex marriages, warns of ostracism and violence, and vows a five-year campaign against it.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (missing from cache); the underlying 2016 report documents the NHTL asking Parliament to review the constitutional clause protecting people against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

GroundUp (6 January 2020) reports that Portia Mtsweni, a 25-year-old lesbian, was found dead — half naked with stab wounds — near Zamani Primary School in Tweefontein, Mpumalanga, in the early hours of Sunday 29 December 2019, and that on 2 January about 800 people marched in the Thembisile Hani Local Municipality in protest, organised by Lasiphumakhona LGBTI, the ANC Women's League and others. Thembisile Hani mayor Nomsa Mtsweni called on parents, leaders and churches to stand united against gender-based violence. The report documents a deadly anti-LGBTIQ incident and local community mobilisation inside Mpumalanga — province-level violence data this record's dossier had not retrieved.

MambaOnline (11 September 2014) reports that Mpumalanga's first LGBTI Pride march and celebration was held on Saturday 9 August 2014 in the provincial capital Nelspruit (Mbombela) under the theme 'Moving Forward, Proud, Strong & United', with around 1,000 participants marching from the SABC offices to Nelspruit Plaza and a post-parade picnic at Oorwesig Garden Park. Organiser Joy Kunene said police were 'visible and supportive' and supplied about 20 police and traffic officers to assist, and the march launched the LGBTI Mpumalanga Movement, an umbrella group for the province's LGBTI organisations. The event is direct evidence of a public, police-supported LGBTIQ+ presence in the province's capital, tempering the record's picture of exclusively hostile local institutions.

Ridge Times (29 August 2026) reports that at the Pride Flag Tour held at the eMbalenhle Sasol Club on 18 August, LGBTIQ+ community members led by the Rainbow Seed Institute raised concerns about alleged discrimination and stigmatisation at government institutions, particularly police stations; participants said they were ridiculed, questioned or treated unfairly when seeking assistance, and one member alleged that after being sexually assaulted in eMbalenhle months earlier, an officer at eMbalenhle Police Station asked why she 'didn't fight back'. Attendees said they fear reporting crimes because of stigmatisation. The report, from the Secunda-area local press, documents current, province-specific LGBTIQ+ grievances about police treatment in Mpumalanga — the kind of enforcement-facing finding this record lacked.

records.name: Limpopo
records.current_summary: Limpopo's rural life runs through chiefs and traditional courts to a degree that makes the parallel customary-law system the province's defining risk factor. Human Rights Watch's analysis of the legislation at issue warned that it 'establishes a separate legal system for people living in the former Bantustans' and 'threatens to undermine this security for millions of South Africans living in rural areas', 'particularly for the exercise of gender and sexual rights' — because chiefs and traditional courts adjudicate personal-status and morality-adjacent matters under customary law, with a consent presumption running against the individual. The later record, from a 2025 verification pass: the bill was enacted as the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act of 2019, and was then declared unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court in 2023, with the declaration suspended and the Act's validity extended while Parliament works on a replacement. A 2012 activist report — 'culture of the chiefs threatens our rights' — pressed the same case contemporaneously.  No statute criminalises a visitor's expression here and no trans-specific incident series is recorded. But for an outed visitor in rural Limpopo, the practical moral authority is often the chief's court rather than the ordinary court — and that jurisdiction's record on gender and sexuality runs against the individual. The absence of recorded incidents reflects under-reporting, not demonstrated safety.

sources.claim: HRW (29 May 2012): the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament threatened LGBT South Africans by creating a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustans; HRW reports rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas, and the bill offered no opt-out from customary jurisdiction. Supports the province's framing of traditional-court rural jurisdiction as the defining risk factor for LGBT travellers off the main cities.

Mamba Online (18 Apr 2012, Melanie Judge): the Traditional Courts Bill debated in provincial public hearings would re-criminalise gay and lesbian conduct in former-Bantustan areas through a separate customary system; lesbians are reported punished at chiefs' homesteads and tribal offices with no opt-out, so those who can are expected to leave rural areas; traditional leaders also opposed the 2006 Civil Union Act. Direct support for the record's rural-traditional-courts risk assessment.

records.name: Gauteng
records.current_summary: Gauteng — the province containing Johannesburg and Pretoria — is where the country's protections are most visibly operational. It hosts the first representative quantitative study of hate crimes against gay and lesbian people ever conducted anywhere in this country (2003/04, by an LGBT well-being institute with a university applied-psychology centre, documenting prevalence, consequences and contributing factors, with the era's leading community organisations as partners). A 2016 national campaign review confirms only three such studies exist in the country's history, placing Gauteng squarely in the small tier of provinces where the evidence, reporting channels and NGO capacity demonstrably exist. There is no province-specific ban or enforcement action here: the national constitution enumerates sexual orientation, and the equality statute and hate-crime framework operate uniformly, with the courts, prosecutors and civil society that apply them most concentrated in this province.  One caveat cuts both ways: the province's comparatively high recorded hate-crime volume — the very reason the evidence exists — may partly reflect better reporting infrastructure rather than greater danger. The operational conclusion stands either way: an incident a visitor reports here is likeliest to meet a functioning institutional response.

sources.claim: 'Hate Crimes Against Gay and Lesbian People in Gauteng: Prevalence, Consequences and Contributing Factors' - Joint Working Group research initiative conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being with the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology (authors Wells & Polders), the first representative quantitative provincial hate-crime study in South Africa (2003/04); partner roster includes Behind the Mask, Triangle Project, GALA and the Durban Lesbian & Gay Community & Health Centre.

Love Not Hate campaign research (GALA-hosted, conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being, 2016): the companion review of hate crimes against LGBT people in South Africa states that only three quantitative studies have ever been done - the 2003 empowerment study across Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape; a 2010 North West province study; and this national campaign study - and measures levels of discrimination against LGBT people nationally.

Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old transgender woman originally from Soshanguve and living in Winterveld (both in Tshwane, Gauteng), was assaulted at a local tavern at about 1:30 am on 26 December 2024 after a man began saying gay and lesbian people 'don't deserve to live'; he smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette, saying 'I told you I'm gonna kill you', leaving deep cuts to her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead that were stitched after treatment at Kgabo Clinic. She opened an assault case at Dube Police Station, which MambaOnline (6 January 2025) reported had shown no progress. The province's most recent documented trans-specific hate incident on record.

The SA Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism (14 November 2025) welcomed the judgment of the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075), delivered on 10 November 2025. The court found the Department of Correctional Services engaged in unfair discrimination and harassment of the transgender inmate by refusing to allow her to express her gender identity and denying her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy, and held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense, ordering the DCS to implement accommodations and enforce its own SOPs. Demonstrates an operational Gauteng court remedy, under PEPUDA, for discrimination against a trans person.

records.name: Chechnya
records.current_summary: Chechnya's security apparatus operates outside legal constraint on this question. In February 2017, law-enforcement and security officials launched an anti-gay purge: dozens of men were rounded up and held in unofficial detention facilities, starved and tortured; some were forcibly disappeared; others were returned to their families 'barely alive from beatings' after their captors exposed them to relatives encouraged to carry out honour killings (Human Rights Watch, 2017). Independent domestic reporting in January 2019 found the persecution resuming and the documented secret facility active again, while the regional leader's press office denied such sites exist. Since 2022, two investigations have documented detained homosexual men blackmailed into 'volunteering' for front-line conscription in Russia's war in Ukraine (at least seven sent, one killed) and a mass wave of unlawful detentions tied to forced mobilisation. The UK Home Office note (June 2025) records systematic campaigns in this republic and the wider North Caucasus from 2017 to 2024 — abductions, torture, extrajudicial killings — and assesses trans people and visible advocates as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with such violence spreading beyond the region after the 2023 'extremist movement' designation.  For a discovered or outed visitor: detention without legal process, torture, coerced conscription or death, with no functioning judicial remedy.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (26 May 2017): documents the Feb 2017 Chechen police purge — men believed gay rounded up, held in unofficial detention facilities for days, humiliated, starved and tortured; some forcibly disappeared, others returned to families 'barely alive from beatings', captors outing them and urging honour killings. Report shows Kadyrov's denial notwithstanding that top regional officials knew. The core sourced basis for this record's extreme-risk profile.

Novaya Gazeta (11 Jan 2019, Russian): learned of renewed persecution of gay men in Chechnya — warnings circulated via VKontakte LGBT-group admins telling those still at large to leave the republic; Kadyrov press secretary Alvi Karimov denied the reports. Follows the paper's April 2017 investigation into torture and killings of gay men for which no criminal case was opened. Establishes the purge reactivated within two years, not a one-off.

The Insider (4 Sep 2024): SK SOS reports Chechen security forces coercing detained gay men into military service — at least seven sent to frontlines in Ukraine, one already killed; methods began before the 21 Sep 2022 mobilisation order. In early Sep 2022 six men were detained on suspicion of homosexuality, threatened with fabricated charges and warned they'd be sent to front. Establishes detention-to-frontline blackmail as an ongoing persecution vector since 2022.

OC Media (Memorial Human Rights Centre investigation): a mass wave of unlawful detentions sweeping Chechnya with detainees forcibly sent to fight in Ukraine — people detained over minor pretexts (missing insurance documents), taken to police departments, subjected to psychological pressure and physical abuse, forced to sign contracts; families sometimes must recruit two 'volunteers' to free a detained relative. Complements the gay-specific coercion reports: conscription machinery as a generalised coercive tool of the Chechen security apparatus.

UK Home Office country policy note, Russia, SOGI (June 2025): records systematic anti-LGBT campaigns across this republic and the wider North Caucasus 2017–2024 (abductions, torture, extrajudicial killings); assesses that in the North Caucasus trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; notes the 2023 'extremist organisation' designation of the international LGBT+ movement exposing support/activity to 2–6 years (organising 6–10) imprisonment, with violence spreading beyond the region. The freshest official-assessment source for the record's trans-specific claim.

records.name: Dagestan
records.current_summary: The UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025) identifies the North Caucasus — including Dagestan — as a zone where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, documenting systematic campaigns by Chechen and North-Caucasus authorities between 2017 and 2024 including abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings. North Caucasus SOS's director states there is “no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus”, that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families, and that the situation worsens year on year.  Canada's travel advisory tells travellers to avoid all travel to Russia, names Dagestan among the republics where terrorist attacks are frequent, and warns that special permission from the Ministry of the Interior is required to enter certain areas — an access regime that also hampers independent monitoring of how state and customary authority operate on the ground.  For a visitor the risk here is the regional pattern: the federal ‘extremist’ designation of 2023, which extended violence in detention beyond the region, combined with local security structures and family-honour norms that produce extrajudicial responses unmediated by legal process. No separate Dagestan-specific written law targeting trans people exists, and no Chechnya-scale documented purge infrastructure is attributed to this republic.

sources.claim: UK Home Office country policy note, Russia, SOGI (June 2025): names the North Caucasus — including Dagestan — as a zone where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; documents systematic campaigns by Chechen and North-Caucasus authorities 2017–2024 (abductions, torture, extrajudicial killings); assesses trans people and visible advocates specifically. Freshest official assessment anchoring this record's regional-pattern claim.

Global Affairs Canada Russia advisory (retrieved for this review): advises avoid all travel; flags frequent terrorist attacks in the republics of Chechnya, Dagestan, Ingushetia and Stavropol Krai; states special permission from the Ministry of the Interior is required to enter certain areas and regions; and warns violence targeting 2SLGBTQI+ persons occurs, particularly in the North Caucasus republics of Chechnya and Dagestan. The record's access-regime claim (MOI permission hampering monitoring) comes from here.

Human Rights House Foundation interview with David Isteev (North Caucasus SOS, working in exile): 'There is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families'; situation worsens year on year. Testimony-based regional assessment underpinning this record's 'no safe private existence' line.

records.name: Ingushetia
records.current_summary: The UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025) treats the North Caucasus as the exception to its general finding on Russia: people in the region, trans people, and public LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, and systematic campaigns against LGBT+ people by Chechen and North-Caucasus authorities from 2017 to 2024 included abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings. North Caucasus SOS states there is “no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus”, where even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families.  Canada's advisory against all travel to Russia names Ingushetia among the republics where terrorist attacks are frequent and warns that entering certain areas requires special permission from the Ministry of the Interior; the special-access regime also limits independent monitoring. Like neighbouring Dagestan, Ingushetia has no documented republic-specific purge infrastructure on the scale recorded for Chechnya.  The risk for a discovered visitor is federal hostility operating through local security structures and family-honour norms — extrajudicial responses unmediated by legal process — rather than any Ingushetia-specific written provision against trans people.

sources.claim: Global Affairs Canada Russia advisory (retrieved for this review): advises avoid all travel; lists Ingushetia among republics with frequent terrorist attacks (with Chechnya, Dagestan, Stavropol Krai); notes foreigner surveillance and specifically that 2SLGBTQI+ persons, allies and families have been attacked, harassed and abused; since Jan 2024 organisations advocating for 2SLGBTQI+ issues are treated as 'extremist'; MOI special permission required to enter certain areas. Regional testimony underpinning this record's risk framing.

records.name: Kabardino-Balkaria
records.current_summary: The UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025) places the North Caucasus — this republic among them — in the category where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, and documents systematic campaigns against LGBT+ people across the region from 2017 to 2024 including abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings. North Caucasus SOS's judgement that there is “no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus”, with private existence able to trigger violence, detention or forced return to families, encompasses the republic, and the organisation says the situation worsens year on year.  No Chechnya-scale extrajudicial detention or purge infrastructure is documented here, and the republic carries no special-permission entry requirement of the kind Western advisories attach to some other North-Caucasus republics (it is flagged in Canadian guidance only for general security near the Georgian border). The applicable risk is the regional one: the 2023 federal ‘extremist’ designation operating through security structures and family-honour norms that can produce violence and informal detention outside legal process.

records.name: Karachay-Cherkessia
records.current_summary: The UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025) treats the North Caucasus as the exception within Russia: people in the region, trans people, and public LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, amid documented systematic campaigns against LGBT+ people from 2017 to 2024 that included abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings. North Caucasus SOS — which coordinates roughly 34 evacuations a year of people fleeing the region — states there is “no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus”, where even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families.  No Karachay-Cherkessia-specific purge infrastructure is documented. The visitor-facing risk is therefore the regional pattern rather than any locally recorded apparatus: the 2023 federal ‘extremist’ designation, after which violence in detention spread beyond the region, operating through security practices and family-honour norms that can produce extrajudicial outcomes unmediated by legal process.

records.name: Moscow
records.current_summary: Moscow is where the federal anti-LGBT framework is enforced most visibly. The Moscow Times' 2025 survey of persecution — headlined around “arrests, club raids and extremism charges” — records that the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds, Kotov, was arrested in Moscow in late December 2024; the paper reported Russia's first prison sentence under the LGBT-‘extremism’ designation in February 2025, an organising case following a ruling reported from Siberia in January 2025.  The severity of the federal law is uniform across the country, but enforcement intensity is not: Moscow concentrates the highest police density, the most active venue-level operations, and the bureaucratic touchpoints most likely to involve a foreign visitor — document verification, medical gatekeeping, registration procedures. For a trans visitor the practical result is a materially higher probability of encountering active enforcement of the same rules, and the country offers no protective institutional counterweight at any level.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (paywall shell); the underlying Moscow Times report (February 2025) covered Russia's first prison sentence under the LGBT-extremism designation - an organising case, following a court ruling in Siberia reported January 2025.

Wikipedia's Russia country overview records the federal framework a Moscow visitor stands under: the Supreme Court in November 2023 declared the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and on 22 March 2024 it was formally added to the state's unified list of terrorist and extremist organisations, a designation the page says has led to arrests of gay bar owners and of people displaying rainbow-flag symbols on extremism charges. The page also records the July 2023 federal law banning gender transition outright - both gender-affirming surgery and any legal gender recognition - plus Moscow-specific facts: Moscow authorities have never approved a request to hold a gay pride rally, and in 2011 the head of the Moscow Registry Office stated publicly that attempts by same-sex couples to marry in Moscow are "doomed to fail."

records.name: NCR
records.current_summary: The Philippines has no national anti-discrimination statute covering gender identity; the national picture is violence against trans women, documented in a 2024–2025 series of killings, without dependable local machinery. The capital region carries the country's strongest local protections: in July 2025 Quezon City became its first local government unit to enact a Gender-Inclusive Health Ordinance, creating a framework for gender-affirming primary care, mental-health support and specialist services through the city's public-health system — the only enforceable institutional recourse a discovered visitor can find anywhere in the archipelago.  Lethal violence is on the regional record too: the transrespectful memorial lists Shaina Bayabay, 29, strangled during a drinking session in Pasig City, Metro Manila, on 1 March 2024. Protection here is real but partial — a functioning framework on paper in the country's largest city, and an enforcement-and-services reality that does not yet extend past city limits.

sources.claim: Quezon City government: ordinance by Councilors Bernard Herrera et al. makes all city public health facilities offer gender-affirming consultations and counselling, mental health support, and medical guidance/referrals regardless of gender identity or expression; Mayor Joy Belmonte says it removes longstanding healthcare barriers for gender-diverse and transgender residents - concrete municipal-level protection inside Metro Manila.
